meta.headline: Inflation is outpacing wage growth again, squeezing Americans' paychecks

relevance.reason: The article compares inflation with wage growth and shows the effect on household spending, which fits inflation and consumption.

mapping.justification: The main issue is inflation rising faster than wages, which reduces real incomes and purchasing power.
mapping.cross_theme_note: The article spans Theme 2 (inflation and consumption) and Theme 1 (income elasticity of demand and inferior goods).

paragraphs: Prices in the US are rising faster than wages again. Consumer prices were 3.4% higher in August than a year earlier, while average hourly earnings rose only 3.1%. Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings fell 0.1% from July and 0.3% from a year earlier, so workers are losing purchasing power.

An economist at Navy Federal Credit Union explained that wages had generally grown faster than prices from May 2023 until about April this year, but the trend reversed when energy costs jumped after the war involving Iran. The credit union estimated that gasoline prices jumped 21% in March, pushing its measure of car ownership costs to a record. Gasoline rose 3.9% in August alone and accounted for more than one third of the rise in consumer prices, and diesel reached $6 a gallon for the first time.

The squeeze is beginning to affect spending. Consumer spending makes up roughly two thirds of US economic activity, and the economist expects households to become more cautious. Spending data shows people switching from stores such as Whole Foods to cheaper ones such as Costco and Aldi, across almost the whole income range.

The economist thinks it is hard to see inflation falling much while geopolitical tensions continue and wage growth slows. The best case is that wages and inflation converge around the start of 2027, though even that would still feel difficult for many households on the ground.

Real wages show whether households can actually buy more or less than before. When prices rise faster than pay, spending power falls, which can reduce consumption, weaken economic growth and change what people buy. This article links a global energy shock to everyday household budgets and to the wider economy.

concepts: Consumption as a component of aggregate demand
Income elasticity of demand and inferior goods
chain: The war involving Iran pushes up energy prices, and consumer prices rise 3.4% over the year.
Average hourly earnings rise by only 3.1%, so real wages fall by 0.3%.
Households can buy less with their pay, so their purchasing power weakens.
Households cut back and switch to cheaper stores such as Costco and Aldi.
Consumption is about two thirds of US economic activity, so lower spending reduces aggregate demand and slows growth.
Firms selling more expensive goods may lose sales, and the squeeze may last until around 2027.

evaluation.label: Magnitude
evaluation.text: real wages fell only 0.3% over the year, so the squeeze is small so far, although it follows a long period in which wages were catching up.

evaluation.label: Duration
evaluation.text: the economist expects wage growth and inflation to converge only around the start of 2027, so the effect on spending could last many months.

evaluation.label: Who is affected
evaluation.text: the article says the shift to discount shopping is seen almost across the income range, but the effect will differ between households depending on how much of their income goes on fuel and food.

key_terms.definition: Wages measured in current money terms, without adjusting for changes in prices.
Wages adjusted for inflation, which show how much they can actually buy.
A sustained increase in the general price level, usually measured as an annual percentage change.
The quantity of goods and services that a given amount of money can buy.
A measure of inflation that tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods and services bought by households.
Spending by households on goods and services, and the largest component of aggregate demand.
The total planned spending on an economy's goods and services, made up of consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.
A good for which demand falls as incomes rise and rises as incomes fall, giving a negative income elasticity of demand.

questions.prompt: US consumer prices rose 3.4% over the year to August, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1%. What was the approximate change in real average hourly earnings?
questions.explanation: Real wage growth is approximately 3.1% − 3.4% = −0.3%, so real earnings fell by about 0.3%.

questions.prompt: If households cut their spending because real wages fall, what is the most likely effect?

options.text: Aggregate demand falls and growth slows

questions.explanation: Consumption is a major component of aggregate demand, so lower spending reduces AD and slows growth.

questions.prompt: Some shoppers have switched from Whole Foods to cheaper stores such as Costco and Aldi as real incomes fall. Which concept best explains this?

options.text: Demand for inferior goods rises when incomes fall

questions.explanation: Lower-priced alternatives behave like inferior goods, because demand for them rises when real incomes fall.

questions.prompt: Explain how a fall in real wages could reduce consumer spending.

points: Identifies that real wages fall when prices rise faster than wages, reducing purchasing power.
Uses the article, for example inflation of 3.4% against wage growth of 3.1%, or real earnings down 0.3% over the year.

Develops a chain, for example: households can buy less with the same pay (1), so they cut spending or trade down to cheaper stores, and because consumption is about two thirds of economic activity, aggregate demand falls (1).

notes: Award 1 mark for a partial chain and 2 for a complete one.

questions.prompt: Assess the likely effects of falling real wages on the US economy.

points: Real wages equal nominal wages adjusted for inflation.
Consumption is a major part of aggregate demand.
Inflation of 3.4% and wage growth of 3.1%.
Real earnings down 0.3% over the year.
Gasoline accounting for more than a third of the rise in prices.
Consumer spending about two thirds of US activity.
Households switching to Costco and Aldi.

Lower purchasing power reduces consumption and AD, firms see lower sales and may cut investment or jobs, retailers that sell more expensive goods lose demand while discount stores gain, and the effect may be greater if the squeeze lasts.

Judge using the small size of the fall so far (0.3%), how long the squeeze lasts (possibly until the start of 2027), differences between households, and other influences on spending such as interest rates and energy prices.
A supported conclusion should say how serious the effect is likely to be and why.

discussion.prompt: If your pay rises by 3.1% but prices rise by 3.4%, are you better off or worse off? What else would you need to know?
